text: Every function takes data frame names columns plot, strings.

title: Get started
text: line_chart() accepts ts object directly. Hover chart read values, drag zoom, use range buttons navigator : multivariate ts gives one line per column. data frame, give date column x one several value columns y (single value column group column):
code: line_chart(AirPassengers, y = "passengers", title = "Airline passengers, 1949-1960") line_chart(   EuStockMarkets,   transform = "index",   title = "European stock indices",   subtitle = "Rebased to 100 at the first visible date; zoom in to move the base" )

title: Get started
text: Bar charts take one row per category, raw rows count aggregate (agg). data aggregated first dplyr:
code: library(dplyr) library(ggplot2) # for the mpg data  mpg %>%   group_by(manufacturer) %>%   summarise(mean_cty = mean(cty)) %>%   bar_chart(     x = "manufacturer",     y = "mean_cty",     sort = "descending",     ytitle = "Average city miles per gallon",     title = "City fuel economy by manufacturer"   )

title: Get started
text: Every ddplot chart r2d3 htmlwidget, Shiny app can use r2d3::d3Output() UI r2d3::renderD3() server. input changes, chart redrawn place new data options. Interactive state, zoom line_chart() series hidden legend, kept updates.
code: library(shiny) library(ddplot) library(r2d3)  ui <- fluidPage(    h2("Example ddplot application"),    selectInput(     inputId = "colors",     label = "Point color",     choices = colors(),     selected = "springgreen3"   ),    sliderInput(     inputId = "slider",     label = "Point size",     min = 1,     max = 10,     value = 3   ),    d3Output("scatter", height = "450px") )  server <- function(input, output) {   output$scatter <- renderD3({     scatter_plot(       data = iris,       x = "Sepal.Length",       y = "Sepal.Width",       size = input$slider,       col = input$colors     )   }) }  shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)

title: Get started
text: chart htmlwidget, can saved standalone HTML file:
code: chart <- line_chart(AirPassengers, y = "passengers") htmlwidgets::saveWidget(chart, "airpassengers.html")

title: Comparing categories
text: bar_chart() draws one bar per category. Hover bar read value, share total rank. buttons top right re-sort bars (original order, largest first, smallest first) animation. highlight keeps bars colour greys others.
code: library(dplyr)  mpg %>%   group_by(manufacturer) %>%   summarise(mean_cty = mean(cty)) %>%   bar_chart(     x = "manufacturer",     y = "mean_cty",     sort = "descending",     highlight = c("honda", "volkswagen"),     valueFormat = ".1f",     ytitle = "Average city miles per gallon",     title = "City fuel economy by manufacturer",     subtitle = "Honda and Volkswagen lead the field"   )

title: Comparing categories
text: aggregate first. Leave y empty count rows category, set agg "mean", "median", "min" "max" (default, "sum", adds rows ):
code: bar_chart(mpg, x = "class", sort = "descending", title = "Cars per class") bar_chart(mpg, x = "class", y = "hwy", agg = "median", sort = "descending",           title = "Median highway miles per gallon by class")

title: Comparing categories
text: group splits bar second variable. Use Grouped / Stacked / 100% buttons switch layouts; legend hides group click keeps group double-click. position sets starting layout. Stacked bars show total bar, refLines draws target average:
code: bar_chart(   data = mpg,   x = "class",   group = "drv",   sort = "descending",   fill = c("4" = "#4269d0", "f" = "#efb118", "r" = "#ff725c"),   title = "Cars per class and drive train" ) sales <- data.frame(   quarter = rep(c("Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"), each = 3),   region  = rep(c("North", "South", "West"), 4),   revenue = c(120, 95, 60, 135, 90, 72, 150, 110, 80, 170, 105, 96) )  bar_chart(   sales,   x = "quarter",   y = "revenue",   group = "region",   position = "stacked",   refLines = c(Target = 300),   valuePrefix = "$",   valueSuffix = "k",   title = "Revenue by quarter" )

title: Comparing categories
text: Clicking bar sets input$<id>_clicked clicked category group. chosen layout, sort order hidden groups kept chart updated:
code: output$classes <- renderD3(bar_chart(mpg, "class", group = "drv")) observeEvent(input$classes_clicked, {   print(input$classes_clicked$category) })

title: Comparing categories
text: horz_bar_chart() horizontal version, better many categories long labels. features; names first arguments differ (label categories, value numbers). 100% stacked layout shows composition category: Negative values grow left zero; negativeFill gives colour:
code: mpg %>%   group_by(manufacturer) %>%   summarise(median_hwy = median(hwy)) %>%   horz_bar_chart(     label = "manufacturer",     value = "median_hwy",     sort = "descending",     valueTitle = "Median highway miles per gallon",     title = "Highway fuel economy by manufacturer"   ) horz_bar_chart(   data = mpg,   label = "manufacturer",   group = "drv",   position = "percent",   sort = "descending",   title = "Drive train by manufacturer" ) growth <- data.frame(   country = c("Spain", "France", "Italy", "Germany", "Poland", "Sweden"),   gdp     = c(2.4, 0.9, -0.3, -0.6, 3.1, 1.2) )  horz_bar_chart(   growth,   label = "country",   value = "gdp",   sort = "descending",   negativeFill = "#ff725c",   valueSuffix = "%",   valueTitle = "GDP growth",   title = "Annual GDP growth (illustrative data)" )

title: Comparing categories
text: lollipop_chart() lighter alternative bar chart: value thin stem ending dot, keeps chart readable many categories similar values. works like bar_chart(): hover lollipop read value rank, use buttons top right re-sort lollipops. can pass raw rows: combined agg ("sum" default, "mean", "median", "min", "max", "count"), leaving y empty counts rows. group, category gets one lollipop per group; click legend entry hide group, double-click keep group. look set circleFill, circleRadius, lineStroke lineStrokeWidth. Values zero drawn downwards, negativeFill give one: Shiny, clicking lollipop sets input$<id>_clicked category group, sort order hidden groups kept chart re-rendered.
code: mpg %>%   group_by(manufacturer) %>%   summarise(mean_hwy = mean(hwy)) %>%   lollipop_chart(     x = "manufacturer",     y = "mean_hwy",     sort = "descending",     ytitle = "Average highway miles per gallon",     title = "Highway fuel economy by manufacturer",     highlight = c("honda", "toyota"),     valueFormat = ".1f"   ) lollipop_chart(   mpg,   x = "class",   y = "cty",   group = "year",   agg = "mean",   sort = "descending",   valueFormat = ".1f",   title = "City miles per gallon, 1999 and 2008" ) change <- data.frame(   country = c("Spain", "France", "Italy", "Germany", "Poland", "Sweden"),   growth  = c(2.4, 0.9, -0.3, -0.6, 3.1, 1.2) )  lollipop_chart(   change,   x = "country",   y = "growth",   negativeFill = "#ff725c",   valueSuffix = "%",   ytitle = "GDP growth",   title = "Annual GDP growth",   circleRadius = 8,   lineStroke = "#c9ced6" )

text: horz_lollipop() horizontal version, many categories long labels. takes arguments, label value instead x y. Counting rows, average reference line:

title: Comparing categories
text: dumbbell chart (also called connected dot plot) shows two values per category dots joined horizontal line. clearest way communicate gap change two groups, time points, conditions across many categories , grouped bar chart require much visual scanning reach conclusion. New York Times Economist use format regularly. chart works equally well comparing two conditions within time period. compare average city highway fuel economy across vehicle classes using mpg dataset:
code: life_exp <- data.frame(   country   = c("Brazil", "China", "Egypt", "India",                 "Japan", "Mexico", "Nigeria", "Turkey"),   year_1952 = c(50.9, 44.0, 41.9, 37.4, 63.0, 50.8, 36.3, 43.6),   year_2007 = c(72.4, 72.9, 71.3, 64.7, 82.6, 76.2, 46.9, 71.8) )  dumbbell_chart(   data     = life_exp,   x1       = "year_1952",   x2       = "year_2007",   y        = "country",   x1Label  = "1952",   x2Label  = "2007",   title    = "Life expectancy: 1952 vs 2007",   xtitle   = "Life expectancy (years)",   sort     = "ascending" ) library(dplyr)  mpg_summary <- mpg |>   group_by(class) |>   summarise(city = mean(cty), highway = mean(hwy))  dumbbell_chart(   data    = mpg_summary,   x1      = "city",   x2      = "highway",   y       = "class",   x1Label = "City",   x2Label = "Highway",   col1    = "steelblue",   col2    = "darkorange",   title   = "City vs highway fuel economy by class",   xtitle  = "Miles per gallon",   sort    = "ascending" )

title: Comparing categories
text: slope chart (slopegraph) places two values per category two vertical axes, typically “” “” two different years, connects straight line. steepness direction line tell glance rose, fell, ranking changed. Edward Tufte popularised form Visual Display Quantitative Information (1983) chart government receipts across rich countries, New York Times graphics desk used regularly ever since. Use small--moderate number categories measured exactly two points; many categories many time points, line chart better choice. line labelled category name value ends, labels overlap nudged apart vertically. default lines colored direction (increase decrease). Hover line emphasise fade others. Use highlight tell story categories: rest drawn muted grey give context without competing attention. compare life expectancy 1952 2007 using gapminder dataset:
code: # Current receipts of government as a percentage of GDP, 1970 vs 1979 # (adapted from Edward Tufte's classic slopegraph) receipts <- data.frame(   country = c("Sweden", "Netherlands", "Norway", "Britain", "France",               "Germany", "Belgium", "Canada", "Finland", "Italy",               "United States", "Greece", "Switzerland", "Spain", "Japan"),   y1970 = c(46.9, 44.0, 43.5, 40.7, 39.0, 37.5, 35.2, 35.2, 34.9, 30.4,             30.3, 26.8, 26.5, 22.5, 20.7),   y1979 = c(57.4, 55.8, 52.2, 39.0, 43.4, 42.9, 43.2, 35.8, 38.2, 35.7,             32.5, 30.6, 33.2, 27.1, 26.6) )  slope_chart(   data       = receipts,   start      = "y1970",   end        = "y1979",   group      = "country",   startLabel = "1970",   endLabel   = "1979",   digits     = 1,   title      = "Government receipts as % of GDP",   height     = 520 ) library(gapminder) library(dplyr) library(tidyr)  countries <- c("China", "India", "Japan", "Brazil", "Nigeria",                "Egypt", "Germany", "United States", "South Africa")  life <- filter(gapminder, year %in% c(1952, 2007), country %in% countries) life <- select(life, country, year, lifeExp) life <- pivot_wider(life, names_from = year, values_from = lifeExp,                     names_prefix = "y")  slope_chart(   data       = life,   start      = "y1952",   end        = "y2007",   group      = "country",   startLabel = "1952",   endLabel   = "2007",   highlight  = c("China", "South Africa"),   digits     = 1,   title      = "Life expectancy: 1952 vs 2007" )

title: Comparing categories
text: bump chart shows rank several entities changes one period next. entity smooth line climbs falls overtakes, overtaken , others, circle every period displays rank. Financial Times, Economist FiveThirtyEight use format league tables, polls country rankings: right choice order matters exact values. data must long format, one row per entity period. default bump_chart() computes ranks period numeric y column (rank 1 = highest value, use rankOrder = "asc" reverse). y column already holds ranks, set ranked = TRUE. Hover line make stand . Use highlight bring entities forward grey rest. GDP per capita ranks eight Asian economies gapminder dataset:
code: league <- data.frame(   season = rep(c("2023", "2024", "2025", "2026"), each = 5),   team   = rep(c("Lions", "Tigers", "Bears", "Wolves", "Eagles"), 4),   points = c(80, 75, 60, 55, 50,              70, 82, 58, 66, 49,              65, 78, 72, 69, 52,              60, 74, 81, 70, 77) )  bump_chart(   data  = league,   x     = "season",   y     = "points",   group = "team",   title = "League ranking by season" ) library(gapminder)  countries <- c("Japan", "Singapore", "Hong Kong, China", "Taiwan",                "Korea, Rep.", "Malaysia", "Thailand", "China")  gdp <- gapminder[gapminder$country %in% countries & gapminder$year >= 1967, ] gdp$country <- as.character(gdp$country)  bump_chart(   data      = gdp,   x         = "year",   y         = "gdpPercap",   group     = "country",   highlight = c("Singapore", "Korea, Rep."),   title     = "GDP per capita rank, 1967-2007" )

text: waterfall chart shows initial value built eroded sequence positive negative contributions. bar starts exactly previous one ended. standard chart P&L decomposition, budget variance analysis, “changed ” narrative. optional measure column lets mark certain bars "total", span zero running cumulative sum, making subtotals final totals visually distinct. Hovering bar shows tooltip label, delta, running total. Without measure column every bar simple delta — useful tracking running balance time:
code: pnl <- data.frame(   label   = c("Revenue", "COGS", "Gross Profit",               "R&D", "S&M", "G&A", "Operating Income"),   value   = c(1200, -450, 750, -120, -90, -60, 480),   measure = c("relative", "relative", "total",               "relative", "relative", "relative", "total") )  waterfall_chart(   data   = pnl,   x      = "label",   y      = "value",   measure = "measure",   title  = "P&L bridge",   ytitle = "USD thousands" ) cashflow <- data.frame(   month = c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun"),   delta = c(120, -30, 80, -60, 95, -20) )  waterfall_chart(   data          = cashflow,   x             = "month",   y             = "delta",   title         = "Monthly cash flow",   ytitle        = "USD thousands",   positiveColor = "steelblue",   negativeColor = "tomato" )

title: Comparing categories
text: radar_chart() draws one translucent polygon per series polygonal grid, one spoke per variable. look feel inspired radar chart Chart.js. Polygons grow center, hovering point shows value, clicking legend entry toggles series. variables measured different units, scaleEachAxis = TRUE gives axis scale:
code: players <- data.frame(   player    = c("Ana", "Ben", "Chloe"),   speed     = c(88, 72, 65),   power     = c(60, 91, 70),   passing   = c(79, 58, 93),   dribbling = c(92, 64, 81),   defending = c(45, 83, 74),   stamina   = c(70, 77, 88) )  radar_chart(   data     = players,   group    = "player",   axes     = c("speed", "power", "passing", "dribbling", "defending", "stamina"),   maxValue = 100,   title    = "Player skill ratings" ) cyl_means <- aggregate(cbind(mpg, hp, wt, qsec, disp) ~ cyl, data = mtcars, FUN = mean) cyl_means$cyl <- paste(cyl_means$cyl, "cylinders")  radar_chart(   data          = cyl_means,   group         = "cyl",   axisLabels    = c("Miles/gallon", "Horsepower", "Weight (1000 lbs)",                     "1/4 mile time (s)", "Displacement (cu.in.)"),   scaleEachAxis = TRUE,   levels        = 4,   gridShape     = "circle",   valueFormat   = ".1f",   title         = "mtcars averages by number of cylinders" )

title: Part-to-whole and hierarchies
text: pie_chart() draws one slice per category, share written slice, next leader line slice small. Rows label added , without value rows counted, raw data can passed directly: Hover slice legend entry pull slice see value, share rank. Click legend entry hide slice (shares recomputed without ), double-click keep slice. Clicking slice pulls . Set innerRadius draw donut chart: number 1 fraction radius, larger number radius pixels. centre shows total, hovered slice’s share value: Pies hard read many slices. maxSlices combines smallest categories “” slice (tooltip lists ). Without legend, labels show category names. startAngle endAngle draw part circle, half donut: labels chooses written ("label", "value", "percent"), labelPosition , padAngle cornerRadius separate round slices. fill sets colours (named vector maps labels) colorCategory picks D3 colour scheme: Shiny, input$<id>_clicked returns label clicked slice.
code: pie_chart(mpg, label = "class", title = "Cars by class") energy <- data.frame(   source = c("Nuclear", "Hydro", "Wind", "Solar", "Gas", "Coal", "Other"),   twh    = c(320, 58, 49, 23, 34, 3, 8) )  pie_chart(   energy,   value       = "twh",   label       = "source",   innerRadius = 0.6,   centerLabel = "TWh",   title       = "Electricity generation by source" ) pie_chart(   mpg,   label       = "manufacturer",   maxSlices   = 7,   innerRadius = 0.55,   startAngle  = -90,   endAngle    = 90,   legend      = FALSE,   title       = "Cars by manufacturer" ) pie_chart(   energy,   value         = "twh",   label         = "source",   labels        = c("label", "value"),   labelPosition = "outside",   legend        = FALSE,   padAngle      = 0.02,   cornerRadius  = 4,   highlight     = "Wind",   colorCategory = "Set2",   valueSuffix   = " TWh" )

title: Part-to-whole and hierarchies
text: treemap shows part--whole data nested rectangles whose areas proportional value. Ben Shneiderman invented technique early 1990s. became famous SmartMoney’s “Map Market” New York Times’ graphics US federal budget. Use many parts (optionally grouped categories) want see glance ones dominate total. supply group column, tiles coloured group group gets header showing total. Hover tile see value share total. Labels truncated hidden automatically tile small fit , chart stays readable even many rectangles. example , 142 countries small label, can hover tile identify .
code: budget <- data.frame(   department = c("Hospitals", "Primary care", "Public health",                  "Schools", "Universities", "Vocational training",                  "Army", "Navy", "Air force",                  "Roads", "Railways", "Airports",                  "Pensions", "Unemployment", "Family benefits"),   ministry   = c("Health", "Health", "Health",                  "Education", "Education", "Education",                  "Defence", "Defence", "Defence",                  "Transport", "Transport", "Transport",                  "Social security", "Social security", "Social security"),   spending   = c(5200, 2100, 800,                  3900, 1800, 600,                  2300, 1400, 1700,                  1500, 1100, 400,                  7400, 1900, 1300) )  treemap_chart(   data        = budget,   value       = "spending",   label       = "department",   group       = "ministry",   valueFormat = "$,.0f",   title       = "Where the money goes (millions)" ) library(gapminder)  pop_2007 <- gapminder[gapminder$year == 2007, ]  treemap_chart(   data        = pop_2007,   value       = "pop",   label       = "country",   group       = "continent",   valueFormat = ".3~s",   padding     = 1,   title       = "World population in 2007" )

title: Part-to-whole and hierarchies
text: waffle chart grid squares, 10 x 10 default, category fills number cells proportion share whole. 100 cells, square reads one percent, “third” “fewer one ten” visible glance. Readers find easier judge pie slices. Pew Research Center, FiveThirtyEight, Economist Washington Post use format often, R popularised Bob Rudis’s waffle package. Use handful categories make single whole, survey responses, vote shares budget splits. Cells allocated largest-remainder method, counts always add exactly number cells. Hover cell legend entry highlight category. can change grid size rows cols, fill order direction = "col". example shows continent’s share world population 2007 10 x 20 grid, cell half percent:
code: survey <- data.frame(   response = c("Strongly agree", "Agree", "Neutral",                "Disagree", "Strongly disagree"),   n = c(312, 405, 158, 87, 38) )  waffle_chart(   data     = survey,   category = "response",   value    = "n",   colors   = c("#1a9641", "#a6d96a", "#bdbdbd", "#fdae61", "#d7191c"),   title    = "Do you support the new policy?" ) library(gapminder)  pop_2007 <- gapminder[gapminder$year == 2007, ] pop_continent <- aggregate(pop ~ continent, data = pop_2007, FUN = sum)  waffle_chart(   data      = pop_continent,   category  = "continent",   value     = "pop",   direction = "col",   rows      = 10,   cols      = 20,   title     = "World population by continent, 2007" )

title: Part-to-whole and hierarchies
text: sunburst_chart() draws hierarchical data concentric rings. inspired signature sunburst chart Apache ECharts reimplemented plain D3. Hover sector highlight branch, click zoom , click centre zoom back . Without value column, sectors sized row counts:
code: library(gapminder)  pop_2007 <- gapminder[gapminder$year == 2007, ]  sunburst_chart(   data        = pop_2007,   levels      = c("continent", "country"),   value       = "pop",   valueFormat = ".3~s",   rootLabel   = "World",   title       = "World population in 2007" ) sunburst_chart(   data        = mpg,   levels      = c("class", "manufacturer"),   rootLabel   = "Cars",   labelRotate = "tangential",   title       = "Number of car models by class and manufacturer" )

title: Part-to-whole and hierarchies
text: mosaic_chart() draws mosaic (Marimekko) chart, inspired mosaic example Vega-Lite gallery. column’s width category’s share total, column split segments add 100%, every cell’s area proportional count. Hover cell see count, column’s share share within column. value omitted, rows counted. Factor levels set order columns segments:
code: titanic <- as.data.frame(Titanic)  mosaic_chart(   data   = titanic,   x      = "Class",   fill   = "Survived",   value  = "Freq",   colors = c("#e45756", "#4c78a8"),   xtitle = "Share of passengers and crew",   ytitle = "Share within class",   title  = "Who survived the Titanic?" ) cars <- mtcars cars$cyl  <- factor(cars$cyl,  levels = c(8, 6, 4), labels = c("8 cyl", "6 cyl", "4 cyl")) cars$gear <- factor(cars$gear, levels = c(3, 4, 5), labels = c("3 gears", "4 gears", "5 gears"))  mosaic_chart(cars, x = "cyl", fill = "gear", labelType = "both",              legendTitle = "Gears", title = "Motor Trend cars: gears by cylinders")

title: Part-to-whole and hierarchies
text: rose_chart() draws Nightingale rose, also called coxcomb polar area chart. inspired polar-interval rose chart AntV G2. Every category gets wedge angle, radius follows square-root scale wedge’s area stays proportional value. optional group column stacks wedges. example uses Florence Nightingale’s monthly death counts Crimean War, 1854–55 (values HistData::Nightingale). Use sort order wedges size:
code: mon <- c("Apr 1854", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov",          "Dec", "Jan 1855", "Feb", "Mar") crimea <- data.frame(   month  = factor(rep(mon, times = 3), levels = mon),   cause  = factor(rep(c("Preventable disease", "Wounds", "Other causes"), each = 12),                   levels = c("Preventable disease", "Wounds", "Other causes")),   deaths = c(1, 12, 11, 359, 828, 788, 503, 844, 1725, 2761, 2120, 1205,              0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 81, 132, 287, 114, 83, 42, 32,              5, 9, 6, 23, 30, 70, 128, 106, 131, 324, 361, 172) )  rose_chart(   data     = crimea,   category = "month",   value    = "deaths",   group    = "cause",   colors   = c("#7fa7c9", "#e0645c", "#4d4d4d"),   title    = "Causes of death in the army in the East, 1854-55",   height   = 560 ) rose_chart(   data        = data.frame(state = rownames(USArrests)[1:12],                            murder = USArrests$Murder[1:12]),   category    = "state",   value       = "murder",   sort        = "desc",   valueFormat = ".1f",   title       = "Murder arrests per 100,000 residents (1973)" )

title: Distributions
text: histogram() shows numeric variable spread, bars counting observations bins equal width. Give vector, data frame name column. bins get round widths, summary data (number observations, mean, median, standard deviation) shown bars. chart interactive: − / + buttons change number bins, Count / % switches counts percentages; hovering bin shows range, count, share total share observations bin; dragging across bars selects range, summary describes selected observations. Zoom re-bins data inside range (useful long tails); double-click go back. Add density curve density = TRUE ("normal" fitted normal curve), mean median lines stats, thresholds refLines. binWidth sets width bins, xPrefix, xSuffix xFormat format values: group, bars split group, stacked overlaid (switch buttons). stat = "percent" overlaid groups divides group size, groups different sizes can compared. Click legend entry hide group, double-click isolate : breaks gives bins unequal widths (bars show densities, areas stay comparable), rug = TRUE draws tick every observation: Shiny, input$<id>_clicked returns clicked bin input$<id>_selected selected range.
code: histogram(   x      = mpg$hwy,   title  = "Highway fuel economy",   xtitle = "Miles per gallon" ) histogram(   x        = "price",   data     = diamonds,   bins     = 50,   density  = TRUE,   stats    = c("mean", "median"),   xPrefix  = "$",   xFormat  = ",.0f",   title    = "Diamond prices",   subtitle = "Drag across the bars to select a range, then zoom in" ) histogram(   x        = "hwy",   data     = mpg,   group    = "drv",   position = "overlay",   stat     = "percent",   binWidth = 2,   density  = TRUE,   fill     = c("4" = "#4269d0", f = "#efb118", r = "#ff725c"),   title    = "Highway fuel economy by drive train" ) histogram(   x       = faithful$eruptions,   breaks  = c(1.5, 2, 2.5, 3.5, 4, 4.5, 5.5),   rug     = TRUE,   title   = "Old Faithful eruptions",   xtitle  = "Duration (minutes)",   xSuffix = " min" )

title: Distributions
text: violin_plot() reproduces look Plotly.js violin traces. group gets mirrored kernel density, optional inner box plot, jittered raw points, hover tooltip showing summary statistics. Use points = "" show every observation, meanline mark mean, sort order violins, scale = "count" make violin’s width proportional group size:

title: Distributions
text: beeswarm plot shows every individual data point along numeric axis, spreading sideways never overlap. far transparent box plot nothing hidden behind summary statistic — see full shape, outliers, clusters raw data. New York Times graphics desk uses style regularly remind readers numbers represent real people. layout computed D3 force simulation: point pulled toward true value x-axis collision force prevents two circles touching. group column provided, one swarm drawn per group colored automatically: can swap dataset adjust look freely. using built-iris dataset different color palette larger points:
code: library(ggplot2) # for the mpg dataset  # Single swarm — full distribution of highway fuel economy beeswarm_plot(   data   = mpg,   x      = "hwy",   col    = "steelblue",   xtitle = "Highway miles per gallon",   title  = "Distribution of hwy" ) beeswarm_plot(   data   = mpg,   x      = "hwy",   group  = "class",   xtitle = "Highway miles per gallon",   title  = "Highway fuel economy by vehicle class",    tooltip = "manufacturer" ) beeswarm_plot(   data         = iris,   x            = "Sepal.Length",   group        = "Species",   colorPalette = "Set2",   radius       = 5,   opacity      = 0.8,   xtitle       = "Sepal length (cm)",   title        = "Sepal length by species" )

title: Distributions
text: ridgeline plot, also known “joy plot”, stacks several partially overlapping density curves, one per group, shared x-axis. nickname comes cover Joy Division’s 1979 album Unknown Pleasures, reproduces 1970 plot successive radio pulses first discovered pulsar. Claus Wilke’s ggridges package made format popular, FiveThirtyEight Washington Post use often. good way compare shape many distributions (shifts, spread, bimodality) without space grid histograms need. densities computed browser Gaussian (default) Epanechnikov kernel. default, one joint bandwidth picked pooled data Silverman’s rule thumb, every ridge smoothed way. Lower ridges drawn front ones . Hovering ridge label brings front shows number observations mean. Use overlap control far ridge reaches one , fill, fillOpacity lineCol change look. fill can single colour named vector one colour per group:
code: set.seed(2026)  reaction <- data.frame(   time = c(rnorm(200, 300, 40), rnorm(200, 340, 50),            rnorm(200, 380, 35), c(rnorm(100, 360, 25), rnorm(100, 460, 30)),            rnorm(200, 420, 60)),   condition = rep(c("Baseline", "Noise", "Fatigue", "Dual task", "Night"),                   each = 200) )  ridgeline_plot(   data   = reaction,   x      = "time",   group  = "condition",   sort   = "mean",   stat   = "median",   title  = "Reaction time by condition",   xtitle = "Reaction time (ms)" ) library(ggplot2) # for the mpg dataset  ridgeline_plot(   data        = mpg,   x           = "hwy",   group       = "class",   sort        = "median",   fill        = "#2c7fb8",   lineCol     = "white",   fillOpacity = 0.9,   overlap     = 2,   title       = "Highway fuel economy by vehicle class",   xtitle      = "Highway miles per gallon" )

title: KPIs and monitoring
text: gauge_chart() function renders speedometer-style gauge. takes single numeric value displays circular dial spanning min max. arc divided three zones: normal (plain), warning, danger, color. can adjust thresholds colors match context. warning zone starts 60% danger zone 80%: gauge limited percentages, numeric range works. example monitoring server response time milliseconds, anything 400 ms warning 700 ms critical:
code: gauge_chart(   value = 8,   title = "Memory" ) gauge_chart(   value = 72,   min = 0,   max = 100,   title = "CPU Load",   warningZone  = 60,   warningColor = "orange",   dangerZone   = 80,   dangerColor  = "red" ) gauge_chart(   value = 530,   min = 0,   max = 1000,   title = "Response (ms)",   warningZone  = 400,   warningColor = "orange",   dangerZone   = 700,   dangerColor  = "red" )

title: KPIs and monitoring
text: bullet_chart() function renders bullet chart — compact alternative gauge charts designed Stephen . displays one actual value (dark bar) shaded qualitative bands (e.g. poor / satisfactory / good) optional target marker (short vertical line). ranges argument defines upper bound band; first band starts min (default 0). Colors default sequence grays darker (lower range) lighter (higher range). can stack several bullet charts side side compare multiple KPIs glance: lower value better (e.g. response time), simply order rangeColors lightest (best, lowest range) darkest (worst, highest range):
code: bullet_chart(   value    = 270,   target   = 300,   ranges   = c(150, 225, 350),   title    = "Revenue",   subtitle = "USD thousands" ) bullet_chart(   value      = 7.4,   target     = 8.0,   ranges     = c(4, 7, 10),   title      = "Satisfaction",   subtitle   = "out of 10",   valueColor = "steelblue" ) bullet_chart(   value       = 320,   target      = 250,   ranges      = c(200, 500, 1000),   rangeColors = c("#f0f0f0", "#d9d9d9", "#bdbdbd"),   title       = "Response",   subtitle    = "ms" )

title: KPIs and monitoring
text: liquid_chart() renders single value circle filled animated liquid. water rises empty target level load, two staggered wave layers give surface natural depth, label text switches color water line — appearing textColor surface waveTextColor inside water. Colors, wave behaviour, label configurable:

text: lower upper draw confidence forecast ribbon around line. Holt-Winters forecast base R’s stats package: rollmean draws trailing moving average raw series, kept faint line (showRaw = FALSE hides ). Missing values leave gaps lines: options include yScale = "log", yZero, dateFormat, turning navigator, rangeButtons, zoom, legend, endLabels animate.
code: fit <- HoltWinters(log(AirPassengers)) fc <- predict(fit, n.ahead = 24, prediction.interval = TRUE)  passengers <- rbind(   data.frame(date = zoo::as.Date(time(AirPassengers)),              value = as.numeric(AirPassengers), lo = NA, hi = NA,              series = "Observed"),   data.frame(date = zoo::as.Date(time(fc)), value = exp(fc[, "fit"]),              lo = exp(fc[, "lwr"]), hi = exp(fc[, "upr"]),              series = "Forecast") )  line_chart(   passengers,   x = "date", y = "value", group = "series",   lower = "lo", upper = "hi",   colors = c(Observed = "#4269d0", Forecast = "#ff725c"),   events = c("Forecast starts" = as.Date("1961-01-01")),   valueFormat = ",.0f",   title = "Airline passengers: Holt-Winters forecast" ) set.seed(3) samples <- data.frame(   time = seq(as.POSIXct("2026-03-01 09:00", tz = "UTC"), by = "5 min", length.out = 400),   cpu  = 40 + cumsum(rnorm(400)),   mem  = 60 + cumsum(rnorm(400, 0, 0.5)) ) samples$cpu[150:170] <- NA # a monitoring outage  line_chart(   samples,   x = "time",   y = c("cpu", "mem"),   rollmean = 12,   hlines = c(SLA = 70),   valueSuffix = "%",   title = "Server load",   subtitle = "5-minute samples with a 1-hour moving average" )

code: set.seed(2026) years  <- 1980:2020 genres <- c("Rock", "Pop", "Hip hop", "Electronic", "Country",             "R&B", "Jazz", "Metal", "Reggae", "Latin") peaks  <- c(1984, 1999, 2012, 2008, 1993, 2003, 1981, 1990, 1986, 2018) sizes  <- c(60, 55, 70, 40, 30, 35, 18, 25, 15, 45) music  <- expand.grid(year = years, genre = genres) idx    <- match(music$genre, genres) music$listeners <- round(   sizes[idx] * exp(-((music$year - peaks[idx]) / 9)^2) + runif(nrow(music), 1, 6) )  streamgraph(   data        = music,   x           = "year",   group       = "genre",   value       = "listeners",   valueFormat = ",.0f",   xtitle      = "Year",   title       = "Music genres, 1980-2020 (simulated listeners)" ) phones <- data.frame(   year   = rep(as.numeric(rownames(WorldPhones)), ncol(WorldPhones)),   region = factor(rep(colnames(WorldPhones), each = nrow(WorldPhones)),                   levels = colnames(WorldPhones)),   phones = as.vector(WorldPhones) )  streamgraph(phones, x = "year", group = "region", value = "phones",             offset = "expand", order = "descending", curve = "monotoneX",             colorPalette = "Set2", title = "Share of telephones by region")

text: calendar_heatmap() inspired signature heatmap Frappe Charts GitHub’s contribution graph. draws one rounded square per day week--weekday grid, one panel per year, “Less … ” legend staggered fade-. Hover day see value, legend square highlight every day color bucket. Data spanning several years drawn one panel per year:
code: set.seed(2026) days <- seq(as.Date("2026-01-01"), as.Date("2026-12-31"), by = "day") weekday <- !(format(days, "%u") %in% c("6", "7")) activity <- data.frame(   day     = days,   commits = rpois(length(days), ifelse(weekday, 6, 1.5)) * rbinom(length(days), 1, 0.8) )  calendar_heatmap(activity, date = "day", value = "commits", title = "Commits in 2026") set.seed(1) days <- seq(as.Date("2021-01-01"), as.Date("2023-12-31"), by = "day") season <- 10 + 8 * sin(2 * pi * as.numeric(format(days, "%j")) / 365) rainfall <- data.frame(day = days, rain = pmax(0, rnorm(length(days), season, 6)))  calendar_heatmap(   rainfall, date = "day", value = "rain", weekStart = "monday",   colors = c("#9be9a8", "#40c463", "#30a14e", "#216e39"),   valueLabel = "mm of rain", valueFormat = ",.1f",   title = "Daily rainfall, 2021-2023" )
